utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise again for the late start. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This -- good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue, I put on the record that the witness has worked on a copy of the diagram. It was received by the Registrar only a few minutes ago. It has been given to the Simatovic Defence so that they can consider what -- it has not been given, but it will be given to the Simatovic Defence so that they can consider what to do with it, yes or no. Then a second matter. Mr. Milosevic, I've forgotten to do something which I think I've not forgotten before in the last ten years; that is, to instruct you that you should not speak about your testimony with anyone. Now, to forget this, you couldn't do it any better than when the witness is a professor in criminal procedure, because he might well understand what the position of a witness is. Again, this is not an excuse, but may I take it that you have not discussed your testimony with others? By the way, without an order you would not be under a strict obligation not to do so, but may I take it that you did not discuss the content of your evidence, either given or still to be given, with other persons? Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I should have been clearer in my instructions. Finally, could the parties give any expectation as far as the time needed for cross-examination? Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: At this point I request five hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I thought that under the present circumstances you would agree that Ms. Marcus would be the first one to cross-examine the witness because you were short in time to prepare for the cross-examination; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, any problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And time, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Presently three hours, but the Prosecution have disclosed -- or not disclosed. They are seeking or may rely upon a number of -- many new documents, so it will very much depend upon what happens with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll now proceed. Mr. Petrovic, are you ready, and is your estimate about less than six hours still valid?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe I will conclude my cross -- my examination by the end of the second session today, which is less than my initial estimate of six hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. I -- before I again forget to give you instructions, Mr. Milosevic, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Milosevic. We shall continue where we left off yesterday. In your expert report, you mentioned the rules on organisation from 1990, paragraphs from 110 to 118, and also the rules on organisation from 1992, paragraphs 119 to 196. What is the importance of the rules on work and organisation in the State Security Service when it occupies such a prominent place in your report?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is practically the two most important documents. They are, indeed, bylaws, but their importance is great for the organisation and for the very functioning of the State Security Service, because they prescribe the purview, the tasks, and the description of the duties of each employee, and in that sense these are the most important documents in the State Security Service ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, these two, 2D938 and 2D997, are these the only rules that were in application from 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every particular period, the current rules are in force. At each point in time there is one rule book in place. From 1990 to 1992, one set of rules was in force; and from 1992 to 1995, the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 2D917, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's an appendix to your report, appendix number 5. And when we get it on the screen, could you tell us briefly what we see on this schematic?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are internal organisational units of the state security department at the headquarters, that means the administration in the headquarters. There are eight of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 2D918.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what kind of schematic is this and why we also see here the centres of the service in Kosovo and in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a schematic display of the organisation of the state security department under the rules of 1992. This is the organisation of the service outside the headquarters. We see the centres because the RDB centre is now the main organisational unit, including the one in Belgrade, and we also see the centres in Kosovo and in Vojvodina. Do I need to read it? I don't see very well. I apologise to the Court. Centar, Gnjilane, Pristina, Prizren, Novi Sad, Pancevo, and so on, because under the new job specification the centres of the RDB covered the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia, not only Serbia proper, without provinces. The jurisdictions of these centres did not entirely coincide with some other administrative divisions of the country, but they were functionally organised so as to cover the entire country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain this unification in the names of branches of the RDB from January 1992 compared to the situation before that was governed by the 1990 rules? What are the changes in terminology in the names of branches?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This equalizes all organisational units outside the headquarters. No distinction is made any longer between the centre in Belgrade and -- I'm sorry for speaking to fast. I'll repeat. With this unification of terminology, all the centres of the RDB are equalized in terms of importance and everything else. All the units outside the headquarters are equal. And this is also reflected in terminology and it is also more correct. And each unit outside the headquarters has the same name. Belgrade no longer stands out or above others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what is the difference compared to the rules of 1990, February 1990?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The greatest difference is that the centres are now integrated, too. There are 18 centres and they cover the territory of Serbia proper and the two autonomous provinces, Kosovo and Metohija as well as Vojvodina; that's the most important change. The sectors of the RDB until --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please slow down because only every second word you say is interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is so not true. And unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the interpreters feel that what you just said is unfair. I may take it that it was a great exaggeration, that you mainly intended to underline for the witness how important it is that he speaks slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I apologise to the interpreters. It was not my intention to be literal. I was just trying to say that with this speed of speech, nobody could humanly catch it all. I'm only worried about the record and I want it to reflect everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I summarised in "exaggeration." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sectors of the RDB, until then -- as they were until then, were reorganised and they were integrated in the newly established centres of the department of state security so that all these sectors including the RDB administration for the city of Belgrade, as well as the organisational units that used to be in the provinces, were uniformly organised in one and the same way, which is methodologically more correct, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Could you please look now at paragraph 122 of your report which deals with Article 3 of the rules on organisation from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D997 is the document I would request, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Mr. Milosevic, what is defined by this Article 3 of the rules? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 3 defines the purview of the department. It defines the affairs and the tasks of the department as intelligence gathering, counter-intelligence, standing in the way of terrorism, et cetera, and extremism. And these tasks are singled out as more important because all the other duties are in the category "other duties." So the most important ones are counter-intelligence, intelligence, counter-extremism, and terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just move in the English translation one page further, because the first paragraph of Article 3 is on this page and the more important paragraphs are on the following page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A definition is also given of counter-intelligence, intelligence, and counter-extremism activity, and anti-terrorist activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we look more carefully at paragraph 3 of this article, which says that intelligence gathering and other duties connected to the collection of information, data, and intelligence of interests for the republic in the spheres of politics, the economy, defence, and security, as well as in other areas of importance for the republic, and duties of collecting information, data, and intelligence on all forms of threats to the national and cultural and historical identity of Serbs living outside the republic. Could you please make a comparison between this paragraph in Article 3 and the equivalent passage from the previous rules from February 1990, Article 42 of those rules that is dealt in paragraph 118. And Article 2 of the previous rules deals with activities concerning the national interests of all Yugoslav peoples living outside the borders of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that yesterday. Intelligence affairs -- intelligence work defined in this way includes collecting intelligence about any threat, any form of threat, to the national, cultural, and historical -- historic identity of the parts of the Serbian people that remained outside the Republic of Serbia. This is a transformation of the previous provision to make it closer to the political, social, and historical reality of the moment. This new definition transforms the previous generalised definition that belongs to previous times and some previous cultural heritage. The new definition, in my opinion, is completely adjusted to the reality of the moment, to the current situation, and the actual needs for collecting this kind of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P1043, page 13 in B/C/S and page 20 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It is the constitution of the Republic of Serbia from 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 13 in B/C/S and page 20 in English, straddling page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Article 72 is an article that defines areas that the Republic of Serbia governs and provides for. We see 12 items, and the last paragraph here reads: [As read] "The Republic of Serbia shall maintain links with the Serbs living outside the Republic of Serbia for the purpose of preserving their national as well as cultural and historical identity."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are there any similarities between this constitutional provision and the provision from the rules we had just looked at?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The resemblance is obvious, even in the grammar of it. In my opinion, this is a constitutional principle or a constitutional provision and obligation that was reworded or perhaps even copy/pasted into the rules of the RDB, its definition of intelligence gathering. The identical nature of the two is evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at D115. That is a description of the specified job positions in the RDB from April 1992. Page 12 in B/C/S, and that would be page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document is under seal, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It should not be broadcast then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is a description of the positions included in the job specifications of the RDB from April 1992, and I should look first to the description of the chief position, chief of the RDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Chief of the 2nd Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need bullet point 2. We need the previous page in B/C/S. In English it would be page 7; in B/C/S, 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the first bullet point on this page for you - shall be responsible for performing tasks and duties of gathering intelligence and information of interest to the republic in the area of politics, economy, defence, security, and other areas of importance to the Serbs outside the republic - from which document was this taken, this formulation?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the legal grounds - and I'm not sure I understand the question - it's obviously the constitution of the Republic of Serbia that we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now turn to page 14 in B/C/S and page 8 in English. Bullet point 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could the same be said with regard to the description of the position of the deputy chief of the 2nd Administration of the RDB?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Absolutely the same could be said for that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, given the description of the position of the chief of the 2nd Administration and the deputy chief of the 2nd Administration, the difference between the two is that it says that for the deputy chief he is immediately responsible for carrying out duties. So what does this difference in terminology actually mean in this situation?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, it means that the chief is the person who has the responsibility for organising the work. He has to organise the work and he's responsible for its efficiency, whereas the deputy is directly responsible. That means he's immediately involved in carrying out the tasks and performing the duties, so he ensures that the duties are performed correctly, and that's why he has such responsibility. So he is more personally engaged, more personally involved, in the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We will now move on to paragraph 126 of your report, where it says that the tasks are carried out according to the annual programme of work. The duties in the purview of the department shall be carried out according to the annual programme of work. What sort of work is involved?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the documents concerned are basic documents that provide certain guidelines for action to be taken, but naturally it's not possible to foresee everything that can happen, all the situations that might arise. So these are plans of a general kind that express certain intentions that relate to planned action and so on and so forth. They aren't really specific or concrete because it's not possible to draw up such plans in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the following part of your report, from paragraph 127 onwards, you deal with the rules on the positions according to job specifications. Can you first of all tell us why the rules on organisation is accompanied by new rules on job specifications, if that is, in fact, the case?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's always essential once the rules on organisation have been changed to have a change in the rules on job specifications, because they are new jobs and there is a new organisation, as a result of which the number of staff members changes, goes up or down, and so on and so forth. So these rules depends on the other rules. They are linked to each other. When you change one set of rules, it's necessary to change the other set of rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 129 in your expert report mentions the various sorts of jobs within the RDB - operative, operative specialist, and so on and so forth. What's the relationship between operative jobs and other jobs within the SDB?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in brief, operative tasks are the most important ones. They are the key tasks, that's the essence of the work that has to be done, and all the other tasks, all the other duties that have to be performed depend on operative duties. They are there to make sure that the operative tasks are carried out correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 131, the last sentence of the paragraph is the sentence I am interested in. It concerns the job specifications in April 1990. And in comparison with the previous job specifications, in this case the number of work posts was significantly increased. So why was the number of work posts increased in relation to the situation from February 1990 until April 1992?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all because of the change in the rules on organising work. The organisation of the RDB was different now in comparison to the previous RDB system. The branch units outside the headquarters was greater, so RDB branches were formed throughout the territory of the republic, and therefore it's quite normal that the number of staff members increased, the number of work positions increased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 12, line 13, refers to April 1990. May I take it that it was either a slip of the tongue or a mistranslation and that you wanted to refer to 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in paragraph 132, the rules on amending the rules -- well, the number of staff members was increased by about 500. Can you briefly tell us why this number increased by an additional 500 personnel?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case some staff members, in fact all the existing employees from the SDB of the federal SUP at the time, were involved in a merger incorporated into the RDB of the Republic of Serbia as I said yesterday. And it was therefore necessary for there to be other organisational units. It was necessary for all these staff members to find certain positions within the RDB. And in my opinion that is the main reason for this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll now move on to paragraph 137. Here, mention is made of two basic ways of organising the security and intelligence system institutions. And these two basic ways are the centralised way and the decentralized way. Which method was applied in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decentralized method was applied there. In fact, it's difficult to explain this. If a centralised system is a system where one service covers various duties, well, then, you could say that that was the case in the Republic of Serbia or, rather, in the RDB. In Serbia there was not a particular service for intelligence and a particular service for counter-intelligence work, which is the case in certain other countries. All these duties were performed within a single service, but different administrations were responsible for these tasks. So the system -- the organisation of the system and the service is not the same. I think you were asking me about the service. As far as the service is concerned, it was considered that it would be more practical to perform all these duties in one service. But the tasks were centralised and distributed and, given the principle of secrecy, those performing some duties shouldn't be aware of the other body performing other duties. A totally decentralized system also has certain advantages when it comes to work specialisation in particular, but it also has certain disadvantages and this is a matter for the tactics of the state leadership. It's also a matter for deciding on how to organise things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We have more details about the matter in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at paragraph 142, where you refer to offensive -- the offensive intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you say that they performed the tasks more successfully in the enemy's territory, and it locates its organisational units there. So why are organisational units - sub-centres, points, and intelligence pivots - located in an area outside the territory of the Republic of Serbia in order to perform offensive intelligence work, the intelligence work in those areas?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This concerns all the intelligence services. It also concerns Serbia. So offensive intelligence work includes gathering intelligence on foreign countries or certain organisation, and so on and so forth. So it's normal to perform those duties there, at the source, or in the territory of some third country. Since such activities are performed in a continual matter, it is necessary to perform them over a lengthy period of time. And then for practical reasons it's customary to establish not only intelligence pivots but certain centres, certain stations, et cetera. These were the various terms used in various countries. If necessary, I can provide you with some examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you just briefly make a distinction between intelligence sub-centres, intelligence pivots, and intelligence centres. What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a substantial difference. Intelligence pivots, intelligence sub-centres, and centres, well, they're organisational units. It's a matter of organising these things. Intelligence pivot is a network. There is an intelligence officer who works in the field and all the agents are his associates, and this is called an intelligence network. If they are permanently located in that country, then it's a residence. That's what it's called. So that is something that exists, because that in fact is the most efficient way to obtain intelligence abroad and also to obtain counter-intelligence abroad, because offensive -- the offensive intelligence service is also an integral part of that service and performs its duties abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In these sub-centres, points, and pivots, does one also use a certain operations technology in order to obtain information and intelligence?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only technology and equipment for gathering such intelligence, but one also uses communications equipment. That's one of the purposes of these intelligence points. It has to maintain communications with the home country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll see about that.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, yes. To answer your question directly, my answer is yes, it does also include these technological aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us briefly have a look at paragraph 155, where it mentions the horizontal and vertical organisational principles. Very briefly could you provide us with an explanation of the difference between these two types of organisation, these two principles of organisation?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The horizontal method concerns co-operation between various organisational units at the same level. These are organisational units outside the headquarters and -- that have common tasks and then they co-operate. Naturally, it's a matter of reaching agreements, and so on and so forth. So as for the vertical principle, the vertical principle involves a certain hierarchy and the principle of subordination. The headquarters administration is above these centres, so there is a hierarchy of subordination that I spoke about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 159 -- please have a look at paragraph 159 and tell me whether one method of gathering information or gathering intelligence is lacking there, in relation to the RDB in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is an omission there. I forgot to say "gathering intelligence through technical sources." This is very important now. It's perhaps the most important way of gathering intelligence throughout the world, and especially in technologically developed countries. This is something that is well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what this abbreviation is? Because it hasn't been recorded.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technical intelligence; "Techint" would be the abbreviation. Human intelligence, for example, is "Humint." I hope that everyone's heard of these terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course. Mr. Milosevic, in this very same paragraph reference is made to undertaking secret or, rather, operations actions. What sort of actions are involved?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these actions are usually carried out in the country or abroad, and a significant number of members of the service participate in them. And several sources are used in order to obtain important intelligence or in order to obtain information about certain activities. These aren't ad hoc activities. This is something that is done on a permanent and comprehensive basis in order to shed light on a certain issue and to investigate it in the greatest possible detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 167, this entire part of your report concerns monitoring the SDB's work -- or, rather, the RDB's work. With the adoption of the Law on Internal Affairs in 1989 and 1991, what sort of system for monitoring the work of the RDB and SDB was maintained? We can see that previously there was a method for monitoring their work in the Assembly. But as of 1991, what was the case?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was monitoring through the Assembly. There was a system of civilian monitoring of the work of the RDB and of the intelligence system as a whole, since the Assembly committee for security was concerned with such issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now move on to internal informing and external reporting on the work of the SDB and RDB. It's paragraph 172. It says that the 5th Administration analysis of the RDB concentrated in its work on creating documents of a higher degree of processing specifying a circle of users. First of all, explain to us what is a document of a higher degree of processing created in the 5th Administration?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents of a higher degree of processing are better verified documents. They are based on information that has been verified from many sources. They take the form of briefs and reports. They are the result of operative work and analysis. First of all, certain information is gathered through operative work, then it is verified, compared, referenced, sourced. And based on that information, a report of a higher degree of processing is created and submitted to a number of users.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How is the circle of users of RDB reports defined?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some permanent users, and those were the highest bodies of the state leadership, the highest bodies of authority, and they received a certain amount of information through regular reports, daily or weekly reports. Then the highest body in the Republic of Serbia, that is, the Assembly, that would be briefed twice a year. And in extraordinary cases, external information could be sent to somebody ad hoc, to the public security department or some other body. In any case, it was the chief who decided who would receive reports, but not at his own discretion but according to the rules of the service that were strictly observed, very rigorously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What are the features of a report submitted to external users from the viewpoint of verification, completeness, contents, information about the sources of information contained therein?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: To start in reverse order, it should indicate not only the source and the way -- it should not only keep hidden the source and the way the information was received, but it should contain no information that could possibly reveal the source, and of course the information had to be verified. And external reports should not contain any unverified information except in exceptional urgent cases when -- when initial information had to be provided to somebody, but normally such reports contained only information that was verified very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We -- [no interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel begin his question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, could you restart your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 179 talks about several types of administration in the RDB; operative instruction or operative training, operative analysis and training, operative technical training, and operative organisational training. What does this qualification "training" mean?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the personnel working in these administrations, they did not carry out operative work in the field directly. They trained employees in the centre who were directly involved in such work. So they had great knowledge, they had great experience and skills in certain areas, and they would train operative workers who did those jobs in the field in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would operatives of some training administrations, such as the 1st, 2nd, 3rd one, also able to be involved sometimes directly in gathering intelligence?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any employee of the service, not only of the service, but anyone in the Ministry of the Interior who was an authorised officer, had to carry out any task that he was given. So if an operative situation made it imperative that somebody be involved in a job, and if it was justified and purposeful, of course they could be involved. All the more so because they were more familiar and more skilled than the average person. But that was, of course, up to the leadership of the given administration. It was not prohibited for them to get involved in operative work occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 191. The part that speaks about the relations between organisational units within the department. My question is: Was there any hierarchy among the administrations in the RDB?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were all equal. There was no administration that was superior to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there any overlapping of interests between various administrations or branches in their lines of work, and how would such overlapping be resolved if it occurred?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That occurred very frequently by the very nature of things, but that was solved very easily by agreement between the chiefs at the appropriate level. Some other centre would be informed that they should do some part of the work. It never happened that people arrogated certain competencies or lines of work to them or use them. It was just an organisational matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can we have the foundation for the last answer? It seems not to be based on the rules but to be based on some other direct factual knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the same issue as you raised yesterday a few times, and which I raised, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm asking you: In the spirit of the rules on work and organisation, how would this be resolved? All my questions are framed in this way: How would the rules deal with a situation where information was collected that was of interest for two different lines of work, two different administrations, or where a type of information would be of interest to different lines of work?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely based on the rules. Such situations under the rules are resolved by informing a different organisational unit -- the other organisational unit. But in any case, the immediate superior would provide instructions how to deal with it. In such strictly hierarchically organised state agencies, this could not be a problem. Nobody could or even thought of refusing a task that was given to them. That is in the spirit of the rules, if that is a sufficient answer. So there was territorial jurisdiction. But in case of overlapping of territorial jurisdiction, the higher leadership and the leadership of administrations would decide to give priority to one or the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 216, which deals with the position of the deputy chief of RDB. Towards the end it says, inter alia, deputy chief is responsible for the implementation of self-protection measures in the service. What are "self-protection measures"?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy chief of the department was responsible, and that also means he was responsible for organising certain measures of self-protection. Those were counter-intelligence measures within the service itself, and that is quite normal and natural for that kind of service, because the service needed to protect itself in terms of counter-intelligence from foreign services, from being infiltrated, from planting moles, and thus inflicting great damage. If I may say again, this work was done in great secret for understandable reasons, and that's why the measures were secret as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph 229. It deals with surveillance measures, surveillance techniques. Who would initiate -- who would make proposals for applying surveillance?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operative on that case, in charge of that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To whom would he make the proposal for surveillance, and who would approve these proposals?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the organisational unit or the chief of the RDB would approve surveillance measures. Of course, other chiefs at different levels also had to approve. In other words, it was not possible to go over anyone's head. The whole procedure had to be observed. Of course, technical conditions for putting somebody under surveillance also had to exist, and that was part of the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 231 deals with the methodology of work in the State Security Service. Could you tell me, who defines authorities of the RDB? Who makes decisions about the programme orientation of the service itself?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the RDB, but even if you mean any other service, it is quite clear that it would be the highest political bodies, the highest political executive authority. That means the government, the prime minister, the president; they - along with other bodies outside the service - would provide general guidelines. Those are the representatives of the people and their task -- their job is to protect the constitutional order, so they provide guidelines to the service, including the technical services.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the initiative base in terms of defining tasks of the service?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the initial stage or the preparatory stage in one cycle in which these highest political bodies take stock of the situation in terms of political situation, economic situation, and other aspects of the situation in the country at a certain moment. And based on that they draft an initiative specifying what would need to be done for the protection of territorial integrity, protecting constitutional order, and the vital interests and national interests of the country. That is how the priorities are defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How would these vital interests be defined by political actors? How would they transmitted to the service? How would they operationlised? How are the methods and ways defined for obtaining these goals?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In countries where the national security council or a similar body exists, it could be called a commission of chiefs of services or joint chiefs of services. They would be the first step, the first filter, who would translate these general guidelines into something more specific. But in our country, as far as RDB is concerned, the minister, who is a member of the government and the highest chiefs in the service, would agree about these tasks. And then within the service itself, the tasks would be operationalised based on principles of rationality, efficiency, deciding how best to achieve them. That is how the service would operationalise these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm now moving to a different area. And looking at the clock, perhaps this would be a good moment to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a good moment for a break. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the interpreters told me that if you do not make a pause between the answer and your next question, even your first word will not be translated. They are struggling more with you than with the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I'd like to thank the interpreters, too. I will try and bear that instruction in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just one question that concerns the area we were discussing a minute ago. We were talking about the technology used by the service and authorisation provided for the use of such technology. Did anyone from the judiciary -- was anyone from the judiciary included in authorising the use of technology for the service?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since this is a serious means of tampering with constitutional rights and freedom as a matter of restricting someone's freedom, someone's rights, the president of the basic court acted, because according to the Law on Criminal Procedure he has to participate in authorising such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the court.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The court, the supreme court. It's now called the Supreme Court of Appeal, the Supreme Cassation Court. But then it was called the Supreme Court of Serbia. I hope that this term is a term that is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in your report, in paragraphs 240 to 244, mention is made of gathering and processing and assessing information. And in relation to those paragraphs, I just have a few questions for you in order to clarify the stages involved in the service's work when gathering information is at stake. What sort of actions have to be taken in order to obtain reliable information that can be used and can be disseminated externally outside the department?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it is necessary to gather intelligence, to have the raw intelligence, and this is done by using various means. Live sources, human sources. And then we have technical sources, or it would better say one uses technical means to obtain information. Or information can be gathered from open sources in exceptional case, but this is used more to check certain things. But information is gathered through secret sources, through associates, or through operative technology. That is the first stage. This is raw intelligence that has not been verified. It can be correct and it might not be correct. This has to be checked and determined when further processed. So it's necessary to categorise and check the intelligence obtained. One has to see how logical the intelligence obtained is and how logical it is in comparison to other intelligence gathered by the service or by other sources. And it is only then and on that basis, after having processed the information, that certain information is extracted from it. You have higher level documents in which this information is processed and then this intelligence is conveyed to internal or external users.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How are the sources of intelligence assessed in terms of the weight that can be given to those sources?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several indicators are used. The most important one is the source of intelligence itself. First of all, an assessment is made as to the reliability, the level of reliability of the intelligence. One tries to determine whether the intelligence is reliable, whether it's been checked, whether it's being checked, or one tries to establish whether someone has tried to plant intelligence within the service. So this is one of the most important indicators, but it is not the only indicator. I will slow down, I do apologise. Naturally the intelligence has to be checked. Intelligence or information that is checked can prove to be correct or incorrect, but incorrect information that has been checked can also be important. It can show that information has been planted, and so on and so forth. In certain cases, some information may have only been partially checked, maybe partially correct. So as in the case of all evidence, you check information by carrying out an analysis through induction, deduction, by trying to think about things logically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that the raw intelligence that you have mentioned that's obtained from checked sources are in fact incorrect? Are such situations possible?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Such situations are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could the contrary be the case: You have an unreliable source that provides you with a correct and precise intelligence?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If I can answer that in greater detail. Those two things aren't that close to each other. If you have a source that has been checked, it doesn't mean that the information you obtain will be correct. Perhaps you have a well-intentioned source who wants to provide correct information but he provides misinformation, because information has been planted. Or he has made an incorrect assessment or the source was under the influence of alcohol. There could be many other reasons. It's a matter for assessment. So you have to assess the information, not the source. The source is just a means through which one obtains information, but the information has to be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the raw information or intelligence is only the first stage when it comes to assessing the reliability and the truth of the information provided?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's why this is the initial information provided. You start off with this information. That's the beginning of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What sort of information can we talk about within the department? What types of information?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have operative information; the operative agents deal with that. And you have analytic information dealt with by analysts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you compare these two types of information from the point of view of reliability, which type of information is more reliable?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Analytic information is more reliable because such intelligence is a higher-level intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A pause between question and answer and a pause between the answer and the question. Let's restart with the question you put to the witness, saying: "When you compare these two types of information, when you compare these type of information on reliability ..." And then you started an answer, telling that: "Analytic information is more reliable..." could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such information or such intelligence is higher-level intelligence, so in these cases we have secondary and tertiary documents. Operative information is the primary source. So you have the initial information that you use to obtain other information or processed information but it still hasn't been checked. So it still isn't higher-level intelligence, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to have a look at P079, at that document. I am not asking you about the facts in this document or your opinion about the facts. All I'm interested in is your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is under seal, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is information that was provided to the SSNO security service, September -- the national defence ministry, in fact. And in the penultimate paragraph it says that the source of information provided information according to which Arkan, together with his escort, killed a volunteer. And in the last paragraph, it says that the SUP organs established that the volunteer was being provided with medical treatment. My question is why this document contains this -- these two pieces of information that contradict each other with regard to the fate of that volunteer.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first part of the document, you have the so-called raw intelligence or raw information. The operative agent had write down [as interpreted] the information that he obtained from his personal source. As I said yesterday, he can't change or alter anything in any way. But after that stage in the second part, he stands back a bit because the information has been partially checked. He partially checked some of the information that he obtained. And he determined that with respect to one piece of the information provided -- well, that information was quite simply true [as interpreted]. Then there is the other information that has to be checked. So although it has not been explicitly stated here, these last two paragraphs, or, rather, the last paragraph, in the sentence before the initials, are in fact the opinion of the agent. The agent expresses his personal opinion with regard to the information provided. So I think that what is at stake is quite clear here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now briefly have a look at paragraph 245. Could you briefly tell us how information is conveyed to the users, and is there an established way for handling and conveying information to external users?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally there is a prescribed way that has to be respected. Information can't be conveyed in any other way. The most important external information is provided via courier, and one has to sign for it. And there's a certain manner of handling intelligence; that is to say, the information, or, rather the documents in an envelope that are being -- that is being handed over to a user, these documents have to be returned, and then the document is taken back to the service and it's kept in a safe. So this is a state secret and one has to be cautious. These are documents that can't be sent to users by post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll now move on to paragraph 251. Here factors involved when -- factors involved are mentioned which concern gathering secret intelligence, and one of the factors concerns accessibility. One of the factors is the factor of accessibility. Could you please tell us what the factor of accessibility means within the context of applying the operative technique? What does the factor mean within that context?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Accessibility is the most important factor. According to that factor, the service will obtain the information -- it can obtain the information that is accessible. Operative technology is used so that information that is usually not accessible becomes accessible to the service. So that is the purpose of using such operative technology and other means. So this isn't public information that can be obtained in any other way. It's necessary for the service to have the technical means for obtaining such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: With regard to operative technology and the factor of accessibility, how can you explain the manner in which technological means are set up outside the Republic of Serbia in order to obtain information needed by the service?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's done just as it's done everywhere else in the world. There are two types of operations technology. The first kind concerns planting certain microphones at certain sites. That has to be done on site. You can't do that from a distance. You have to plant microphones in the area that you are interested in in order to eavesdrop on people. If it's abroad, you have to be abroad. If you're dealing with the equipment that is used in order to intercept certain channels, then it is necessary to locate such means at sites where such tasks can be efficiently performed. The closer you are to the source of the intelligence you are interested in, the closer you are to the communications that have to be intercepted, the better it is. Naturally you have to respect the principle of secrecy when acting in such a manner. The communications of the person being intercepted must not be aware of what is being done, so such a system can be established in the territory of a third country or in your own country. This is all a matter that has to be assessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Security factor, what does that mean in relation to what we have just been discussing, in relation to gathering intelligence by using surveillance techniques?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means that you have to ensure that the work you are doing is secret. You have to have physical security so, to speak. What is being done must remain secret, because in other cases information might be planted. There may be this sort of a double-game, if you like. If you discover where the equipment is located, it's very dangerous. It could be very dangerous. So security is of the utmost importance. In many countries, many intelligence services have such centres in military bases that they have abroad so that they can protect their means. They even moved some of those pieces of equipment from embassy to military bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Another factor you mention is timeliness. What does timeliness mean in collecting information by surveillance techniques?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Timeliness is one of the two most important features of intelligence, along with accuracy. Intelligence must be timely, and that's very important. I'll speak more slowly, if necessary. The intelligence service and the state security department always act preventively, to prevent crimes, unlike the public security service which act after the fact. That's why it's important to learn about the plans, ideas, intentions of those who pose a threat to the constitutional order of the country or otherwise pose a threat to the country's vital interests in order to be able to act in good time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information that is not obtained in good time is not completely unimportant. It can serve for purposes of reconstruction, verification, et cetera, but they are less important. It's very important to get some information about the opposite side in good time in order to be able to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next I'd like to ask you relates to paragraph 252. Could you just clear up this concealed intelligence gathering?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is meant is collection of information from open sources, but by trained, skilled personnel who have deeper knowledge, and that's why they can conduct surveillance and monitoring in a more efficient way by, for instance, reading foreign and émigré literature or observing foreign military parades, et cetera. Let me just finish. This is collection of intelligence from open sources but in a way that is not completely open. It is known that somebody is gathering this information but not for which purpose. That's why we call it concealed or covert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We discussed yesterday the rules on work of the SDB from 1992, and you told us that those rules were in force throughout because of their universal nature, and I would now like to look at some passages from these rules. That's D239.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation was admitted under a different number, but I hope we'll be able to display it. For the moment I am interested in para 6, that's page 2 in both versions. Next page in English, please. Item 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Do you see this item?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It says that the RDB may establish co-operation with its own citizens and foreign nationals both in the country and abroad. Does the RDB have any restrictions regarding the place where such co-operation is done or the persons with whom it co-operates?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No restrictions. No service in the world has any restrictions regarding the nationality or the location of its sources. That's simply inconceivable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at item 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the Chamber, next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does this paragraph tell us about the motives of such co-operation with one's own or foreign nationals?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 elaborates on the engagement of foreign nationals. When we say "foreign national," we mean the citizen of another country or an "apatride." Anyone other than a citizen of Serbia. And it specifies motives for such co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What could possibly motivate a person to start co-operation with the agency, in this case the state security department?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any motive could be adequate. Here we see mentioned friendly co-operation, political or other affiliation, as well as other financial or other interests. It also says co-operation may be established with a member of the foreign intelligence service or a military's structure of a foreign country or a foreign organisation, which means that this involves intelligence work in its narrow definition and counter-intelligence. The service can co-operate with a foreign national for any number of reasons, as long as it serves a purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean co-operation could be established with a member of a terrorist organisation as well?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's common practice everywhere in the world. The problem is, however, that it's very hard to infiltrate terrorist organisations, because if it were easier, 9/11 would not have happened. It is ideal if a service has its own member infiltrated into a terrorist organisation precisely for the preventive aspects of its work ante delictum in order to be able to prevent a terrorist act. In any case, that's common practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at item 10, next page in B/C/S and next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It says that the service infiltrates its agent or plants him on an individual or a terrorist organisation when it finds such infiltration to serve a purpose in terms of security of the country and operative interests of the service. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that an agent of the service, a source, not an employee of the service, is planted on the target, gets close to the target in order to be able to conduct surveillance and tailing. Planting or infiltration means that the agent should get as close to the -- as possible to the target in order to be able to monitor them. They should get as close to the target as possible. Become part of their close entourage. Get on the inside, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 60. That's page 7 in B/C/S and page 14 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One page further in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The last bullet point in para 60: Creating high-quality positions for the work of the service under extraordinary circumstances in the state of immediate threat of war or war. What does this mean, the powers of the service? Can it be done both inside the country and abroad?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the purposes of a double combination, and I explained what a double combination is in my previous answer. One of the main purposes of a double combination is to prepare the service for acting in cases that fall out of the ordinary, that happen not in a regular situation but in complex situations, such as in extraordinary circumstances in the state of immediate threat of war or war. Under those circumstances, it is difficult -- more difficult to communicate with agents. Communications are threatened, not secure. And that's why it's important to create intelligence bases and strongholds. It is a very particular situation that has to be planned for in advance in case it becomes necessary, as in contingency planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, paragraph 261 of your report. At the end of that paragraph, the last few words, mention is made of offensive operative techniques and the maintaining of secret communications for special purposes. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are particular ways of communication between the agent and his runner in the service. Because under the principle of secrecy, great caution has to be displayed to prevent the planting of misinformation, and that makes it necessary to communicate in a secure way using specific equipment. That's what "special purpose" means. These communications are agreed in advance. The equipment used is special and the agent is taught how to use it in advance, but of course this has to be used sparingly. They cannot be used for any other purpose, because that increases the risk of detection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about these means of communication for special purposes? Does this activity also include maintaining communications between the headquarters inside the country and its bases in the country and abroad?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the usual way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does maintaining special communication also include self-protection measures at the base of these communications?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered this question already. I've answered that question already, I think. These measures have to be taken at the place where the communications are based. It's very important to prevent detection that could enable the enemy side to use them for a double-game. Let me just remind you: Huge losses were suffered by the Dutch resistance movement during World War II precisely because the Nazi counter-intelligence service detected their communications and managed to play a double-game with them. And many patriots were killed because not enough caution was displayed in handling these special communication devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, paragraph 263. Operative and technical wiretapping means. It follows from this they can be set up both inside the country and abroad. Are self-protection measures involved here as well, at the base from which wiretapping is done of targets abroad?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is used not only in interception but in wiretapping, and protection is always necessary, especially when the target is abroad. It's only logical. Self-protection is always necessary and it's always required to protect and defend the security of these bases, of these communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 264, the last sentence, speaks of covert eavesdropping on telephones and other means of telecommunications that could yield important information for the security and vital interests of the country. What does it mean "information of broader interest to the security of the country"?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means the contents of intelligence. Intelligence work collects information not only on the intentions of the enemy to threaten the security of the country, but information of broader importance to the security of the country. That's common practice everywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 274 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move on, some questions were asked to you, Mr. Milosevic, about the wiretapping. In paragraph 263, we find that wiretapping was applied also in respect of foreign organisations and institutions in the country and abroad. Would that mean that you would have a system of wiretapping outside the boundaries of your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not in a position to know that, and I can't answer your question because I know nothing about that. All I can do is interpret the rules here. However, if you read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- one can see that there is such a possibility, and that is quite in accordance with the Rules of Service. But I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just so -- [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you where in the rule anything is said about wiretapping outside of the country? Is there a specific -- do you need the permission of a judge for that? Or I don't take it that you asked the foreign government for it. Where is the rule about wiretapping abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's in paragraph 263 that we have just been reading. You can see there that it's possible. The procedure for intercepting communications is always the same. I don't believe that anyone acted on their own initiative, and naturally you don't ask foreign countries to authorise you to intercept their communications. No country in the world would act in such a manner. If you want me to explain this in greater detail, there is a pact between five countries in the world, and they intercept the communications established throughout the world, and they don't ask for the permission of any of the countries that they intercept. As a rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. Is your country one of the five?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm interested in the practice in your country, not in what others legally or illegally are doing. What -- if you want to wiretap abroad, how did you do that? How did it work? Who decided? Would you need a judicial order for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as a rule, you needed an order for any type of interception, if this was being done through the usual surveillance equipment. When you're intercepting radio communications, then as a rule you don't ask for authorisation of any kind because you can never know in advance what you'll encounter. So that, at least, is my opinion, but I can't go into all the details because I don't know what the common practice was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, because you limited to radio communications. I was interested in wiretapping, for example, telephones abroad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When wiretapping telephone communications and when planting interception devices, well, you need the same sort of authorisation that you need for intercepting communications in your own country. In our country, the rules apply to foreign countries. That's not the case in certain other countries, but I won't mention them. So the procedure is the same with regard to the traditional type of wiretapping and other types of interception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would get a judicial approval for wiretapping telephone conversations abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How would you technically do that? I mean, would you have intercepts on French telephone conversations or -- you would suspect someone in Paris to engage in undermining activities against your state; how would you listen in to those telephone conversations? Would you seek a judicial order for that in your own country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the technical conditions existed for that, then it would be done. But it's inconceivable, given the technology of traditional interception, it's difficult to do something like that. But it wasn't prohibited. So one would have to proceed as one proceeded, so to speak, on your own ground. Intercepting communications in that manner is a complex affair, and this is done under certain circumstances. I don't know if I have to go into all of the details. It's quite difficult. But certainly I wouldn't contact the French authorities, the French organs, because it wouldn't be easy to obtain their authorisation. Perhaps it would be a matter of international co-operation, but if such intelligence was obtained, then the rule would be to ask for authorisation from the French state, from the French service. But what we are talking about now concerns cases of intercepting radio communications, and such interception can be done anywhere in the -- in the world. But the rules of service don't prevent one from acting in this manner. As to whether it's possible to proceed in that manner, that's another issue. I personally don't believe that it is. I don't know whether such a thing could be done, because it's a very complex matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, one of your earlier answers, when you were still focussing on the radio communications, you said: "Well, I can't go into all the details because I don't know what the common practice was." Does that mean that you're describing the system and the rules without knowing what the common practice was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, common practice, what is common practice? It's difficult to define that. I am trying to provide you with information on the exclusive basis of -- I apologise, I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, common practice. You used the word, so I take it that you know what you meant by using it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My testimony relates, above all, to what one can find in the rules of service and in the rules of work, so I don't know whether something was applied or not. I wasn't involved in that. I can tell you whether something was allowed or not, but I can't tell you whether something was done or not if I wasn't present. Perhaps I haven't understood your question very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you understood my question well and I think I did understand your answer as well. One of the reasons I am asking is the following: We have seen in the various cases before this Tribunal that perhaps not in the whole world always all the rules which prescribe how you have to seek authorisation for wiretapping, telephone tapping, are not always under all circumstances applied, and I was trying to find out what knowledge you had on practice apart from the legal rules on to see whether it may have happened that sometimes, without observing those rules, technical methods may have been used in your country as it may have been done in other countries, even on the Balkans. Was practice always in line with legal theory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They -- there is a crime of illicit interception, and if proof were obtained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that if you violate the rules, that that's forbidden. That's what rules are for. My question was a different one. My question was, and perhaps you have answered it earlier, saying, "what the practice was, I do not know, I only described the rules," which for me, and that's the reason why I put it that strongly, would mean that you couldn't tell us whether the rules were observed, yes or no, because you did not know about what was practice or common practice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to answer that question. But there was an important historical event. It concerned the violation of the rules on intercepting communications, and this affected the course of history, I would say, in Serbia, and it also affected what I discussed yesterday. The chief of police was accused of intercepting the president of the republic and the president of the party, Tito. His name was Plenum, I think. I won't go into whether this was the truth or not, whether this was politically abused or not. But in Serbia much caution was exercised in the matter, and people are very wary of violating the rules on interception. I am not, however, familiar with any cases of violations of the rules on interception. There were one or two cases that involved certain accusations, but I'm not aware of the service being involved in any such cases. I don't have any personal knowledge. The case I referred to earlier was called the Brioni Plenum case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I do understand your answer to be that although you have noticed that there have been cases, and you're referring to case, especially in the past, that there was a case about, whether true or not, a case about illegal wiretapping or telephone tapping, and that you have heard about this at later stages but you have no thorough knowledge of whether this actually happened or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no knowledge of the measures of interception being abused, but this case I mentioned was in 1966. This Brioni Plenum case. It was a historical event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that. Of course, I'm more interested to know whether it happened in the 1990s as well, but you have no factual knowledge about that, and you are -- your testimony is therefore primarily focussing on what the rules were that had to be applied. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to be of assistance in this discussion. Could we have a look at D239, item 37. It should be page 5 in the B/C/S version and page 8 in the English translation. Page 9 in the English translation, item 37. Item 2, in fact, is what I'm interested in here. Could we scroll up in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item 2. It says the technical resources are being used for nationals of Yugoslavia or foreign groups and organisations in the country. Is this the legal basis for intercepting conversations abroad, the legal basis that we were discussing a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what I had to have a look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You should have a look at paragraph 37 -- or item 37, paragraph 2. Could you read it out and could you tell us whether this is the legal basis for wiretapping communications abroad?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Court's leave, with the Chamber's leave, I will now move on.
