utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this a legal basis or is this a rule about the operative and technical resources for something? It doesn't say anything about procedure or ... But let's move on. Let's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Was that question put to me or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it was perhaps a question I put to myself aloud, which perhaps I should not do, but it allows you to read at least some of my mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's just clarify another issue with regard to the relationship between the Law on Internal Affairs and the rules of service. Was there such a relationship, and if so, what was the relationship? What is the law with regard to the work of the service?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of the service are based on a legal act, a legal document. You can see that. If you have a look at Article 1, it says on the basis of the law, pursuant to such and such a law. So these important issues were dealt with or covered by the law, but these other issues, particular issues, that just concern the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the Law on Internal Affairs is the basis upon which the rules on the work of the SDB are adopted?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph 274 of your report. It deals with agents' files. Could you give us a brief definition of the term "agent of the RDB," of the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: By definition an agent, literally from Serbian, a collaborator, who consciously collaborates with the State Security Service, helping the service to carry out the tasks in its purview. It implies also -- it is implied that the person collaborates secretly. I thought that is implied and goes without saying, but now I'm emphasizing it. In an organised way, consciously, and secretly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph of your report it is said that each agent had a file. Who kept these files and who had access to them?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The file of an agent was kept by the runner, as we call it in our terminology. Agents' files were kept in the greatest secret in order to protect the person involved, the agent, but also to protect the methods and techniques of the service. So only the operative running the agent and the chief of the organisation could have insight into the list of agents and their real names. Agents were always referred to by their code-name to protect their identity. Protecting an agent's identity and protecting the agent was a priority in running an agent. The files were kept in a still safe-box. Nobody who did not work with the agent personally was supposed to know. Nobody was able to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have a problem that is perhaps due to my insufficient knowledge of English, and it is with the word "agent," whereas in Serbian it's "collaborator," or I would say "associate." Perhaps this is due to my lack of knowledge, but perhaps not. Perhaps we should clear this up, because "agent" could mean something entirely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you think it -- perhaps together with Mr. Jordash who may have -- I don't know whether the terminology causes him any problem. I leave it to you, Mr. Petrovic, to clarify, because since I do not know where the problem is, I am not in a position to assist you in resolving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the problem either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to clear it up through the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: An associate, is he an employee of the service in active duty or reserve duty?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It could be anyone but a staff member of the service. That person cannot be employed by the service. It cannot be a member of the service. An associate can be anyone but a member of the service. It's an outside associate, an external associate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, your question was about an associate. Did you use the terminology similar to "agent"? Is it -- you used the word in your language which was translated to us perhaps in a different context as agent, and you were concerned about the meaning of the word "agent" to be "acting on behalf of"? Is that what your concern was, and that you thought that by using --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my concern is the colloquial understanding of the word "agent." In my language, it implies a different relationship than that with an associate. It implies that the person is a policeman. It's part of the internal structure of the service; whereas an associate is somebody on the outside of the service, somebody who is not part of the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the word "agent" in English has several meanings. One of the them, perhaps, being in that respect similar to my language, a police officer. Another one is someone who is, I take it, but I should have a look at a dictionary, is working for a company, being an agent working for the company. But I think certainly one of the meanings, and that apparently is the meaning in which it is used here, is that you are working not necessarily on the instruction or being employed by but that you're working and that you work as a link. That you're -- although you're not depending on the institution or entity you're working -- your work is beneficial for, that -- let me check again. I should leave this, as a matter of fact, to the native English-speaking persons. That there is a link, although you're not employed by, you can be an agent preparing, for example, for contractual relationships with -- between parties working, perhaps in favour of one or even both parties and, at the same time, not being employed by them but perhaps being paid for your services you provided to them. So if that's the confusion, then I hope that we have resolved it. It's not someone being employed in the strict sense of being an employee of a labour contract with the institution or the entity, but still work which is beneficial and can assist the party by whom he's not strictly employed. Well, Mr. Jordash, I saw that you are nodding yes. It was a bit of a bad attempt to seek to remove Mr. Petrovic's concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I think, if I can just add, I think what Mr. Petrovic was trying to do was to distinguish the type of agent like James Bond, secret agent, working for the British government, from the situation, I think, described by Mr. Milosevic. I think that's the distinction sought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- to be made. I'm sorry to introduce James Bond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a simple matter, although I do not know by whom he was employed, but a simple example sometimes clarifies matters very quickly. Thank you for your assistance. Ms. Marcus, you know who James Bond is, isn't it? Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we take a break, Your Honour, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we take a break. Mr. Petrovic, where are we when taking a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, unfortunately my estimate was not quite adequate. I will need at least 45 minutes more. I apologise for that, but perhaps it will run even to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check. Madam Registrar, could you provide during the break both the Chamber and Mr. Petrovic with the time he has used until now, and then we'll consider your request for going beyond the second session, Mr. Petrovic. We take a break, and we resume at a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, in view of the time you have used until now and the way in which you conducted the cross-examination [sic], the Chamber grants you this session to conclude your cross-examination -- examination-in-chief, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I would kindly ask you to look at paragraph 279 of your report. It relates to operative actions of the service department. Can you tell us where it is possible to carry out operative actions? Are there any restrictions for the personnel of the department in that respect?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No restrictions whatsoever, if you mean inside the country or abroad. Moreover, operative actions are usually carried out abroad. In the course of the travel of an important official, when a VIP travels abroad, an operative action is put in place to prevent assassination attempts or attacks against that person. Another type of operative action is carried out when it is necessary, as I said before, to collect information from a greater number of persons in a broader area either inside the country or abroad or both at the same time, depending on the scope of the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D239.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's the document we've looked at several times today, the rules on the work of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Para 58; page 6 in B/C/S, page 14 in English. Yes. Now we have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Item 58(c) says that one of the reasons for such an action would be to collect or verify certain information or intelligence of particular importance for the security, the international, economic, or other interests of the country. This formulation, "other interests of the country," which interests could fall under these other national interests in terms of operative actions of the RDB?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any interest. Any national interest apart from those that have been specified before. It could mean protection of Serbs outside Serbia from attempts at denationalisation or restricting their national identity or any other interests. For instance, offensive counter-intelligence could be meant. Anything that is assessed to be of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Speaking of operative tactics of the personnel of the department, are there any situations when an employee of the department, an operative, does not conceal from his source that he's an intelligence officer and does not tell him that he's actually the target, but collaborates with him under another guise?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That could be part of an operative combination. If the intelligence officer approaches the target in order to recruit them, to turn them, that would be a good approach. It is well known in practice. The intelligence officer can also hold himself out to be a member of another service than the one he's actually working for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you call double-combination under the rules of your service?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We are now moving on to the part of your report that relates to the 2nd Administration of the RDB. Paragraph 329. Here we can read about voting on and then proclamation of the Law on the Validity of the Legal System on the Part of the Territory of the SFRY, which was under the special protection of the United Nations. And it was adopted on 18 March, 1992. What happened with the proclamation of this law by the Assembly of Serbia -- of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It relates to the situation that existed since 1974 when republics and autonomous provinces came into existence, if you mean co-operation between services. The co-operation existed before between republics and provinces, and now it is established between Serbia and the territories that are specified here on the same footing as before; that it's on equal footing, in keeping with mutual interests, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this law opens the door for co-operation between RDB services and the services that are created in the territory of Krajina and in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 332. This is the part that relates to Franko Simatovic. A very brief answer, please. It mentions a training course Simatovic completed. What kind of course is that?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a basic specialised course for RDB personnel. It's a course that everyone who gets employment with the service must finish. First of all, they are on trial employment, they pass an exam for a full-time job, and then they complete this basic course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you please explain the following: In the Republic of Serbia MUP and in the RDB, what is the difference between a profession and a work post? What's a profession and what's a work post? What are these terms -- what do these terms cover?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a work post covers certain duties that an employee has to perform. That would be the work post. And the title one has -- the professional title one has to do with a certain rank. The more senior one is, the more experience one has at a certain post, the higher the title will be. But these two things don't depend on each other. They don't overlap. There is no overlapping of these titles and the position one has.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What sort of document regulates these professional titles and what sort of document regulates the work post one has?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The job specification regulates the work post. We discussed these rules on job specifications, but titles are covered by special documents in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs. So these are totally different laws or sub-laws that we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Now let's have a look at paragraphs 333 and 335. In the first paragraph, Simatovic is referred to as the chief of the SAD -- of the USA group in the 2nd Administration of the Belgrade SDB. And in paragraph 335, which concerns the period after the 15th of December, 1990, reference is made to the chief of the department for the US in the 2nd Administration of the SDB in Belgrade. Is there a difference between these two work posts described in these two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no difference. There's only a difference in the name. There's only a nominal difference. But in essence, there is no difference. As far as the work is concerned, there's no difference. It's identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how it is that there was such a nominal difference?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before the rules in 1990, the Belgrade SDB was divided into sectors. And later, after 1999 [as interpreted], it was divided into departments. So it's just a matter of the term used. There is no difference between the sector and department. In any event, there's no difference between these two things. The duties performed were absolutely identical. They were performed at the same level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, here it says -- in the transcript it says, on page 54, line 24, it says that you said "after 1999." Did you say "1999" or did you mention another year?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said after 1990. I said before 1990 and after 1999 -- 1990. Before the rules on the work from 1990 were adopted. I don't know how this error slipped in. Perhaps it was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the year 1999 has nothing to do with what we are discussing here?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. I'm not sure how this error occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 335, it says that Franko Simatovic was assigned as a senior inspector. You've had a look at Mr. Simatovic's personal file. Was this the time at which Mr. Simatovic was promoted to the rank of senior inspector?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's why he was assigned to such a post with such a title.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Simatovic also assigned to the position of deputy chief and special advisor to the SDB? Was he assigned to that position in the same capacity, with the same title?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have a problem with the translation. With your leave, I don't think my question -- I apologise. I see that everything is fine now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. It was the same title, the same post. The position was that of senior inspector, if I have to mention the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And this can be seen in paragraphs 337 and 338 of your expert report; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 351, this paragraph deals with the tasks and duties of the chief of the USA section in the 2nd Department of the USDB in Belgrade. And amongst other things, this paragraph states that as a chief of the department one is involved in performing tasks, in documentation, research, monitoring. So bearing in mind what this paragraph states, does this mean that the chief of the department can directly gather information that has to be processed? And can he cover the field so that -- in accordance with the job specification?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Naturally that can be done. He can do that. That's a logical interpretation of what you have just read out. He can directly perform such tasks and duties. I don't see why that should be in dispute. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the chief of the department for the USA can also travel outside of Belgrade or can travel abroad in order to gather intelligence that relates to a certain subject that has to be processed?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there is such an operative need, the chief can, obviously, act in that way. The chief can directly perform certain tasks. He can assign tasks to others. If his subordinates can carry out his tasks, then he can delegate such activities to those subordinates. But he is in the best position to take action, and he will act as he deems fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As for the position of the chief of the department in the USDB in Belgrade, where is this position actually located in terms of the hierarchy of the SDB?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a low-level position. It's not a very high managerial position. If you have a look at the number of work posts above the post of chief of department, you have several such work posts that are higher-level work posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mention these positions somewhere else in your report. In paragraph 354, which concerns the duties and authority of the special advisor to the chief of the department, does the special advisor have the ability to independently take decisions within the RDB?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the title of this post, you can see that it concerns someone who advises the chief of the department. He advises the highest-level managerial organs in the service, so therefore this means that he doesn't take decisions on an independent basis, but assists the chief to take decisions. He provides advice, but he shouldn't take decisions on his own. Then he would be acting independently. He wouldn't be an advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 355 it says that there are six special advisors to the chief of the RDB in accordance with the job specifications. Are the special advisor positions allocated on the basis of certain fields within the service?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Not really, because this document specifies their tasks in a general manner, but naturally these duties could be shared out in an internal manner. But the rules didn't cover that. They were all authorised to perform all the relevant duties, the tasks. The duties weren't divided in any manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In 356, in paragraph 356, it says that the special advisor also had certain special-purpose resources for which the chief would authorise -- give him authorisation. Who within the service had such resources? What sort of resources are concerned? And for what purposes were these resources used?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the entire managerial team, mid-level and high-level members of the managerial team, had certain resources, and these resources were used to perform one's duties efficiently and to reward associates. So they did not use these resources for themselves. These resources could be allocated to ensure that the work was carried out well, for example, to reward an associate. But all the teams at that managerial level had such resources, had such possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm now moving away from what these paragraphs deal with, and I'd like you to provide me a -- a brief answer to the following: When intercepting enemy communications and gathering intelligence outside Serbia, or when establishing communications with intelligence centres outside of Serbia, what sort of category of intelligence work would such activities be placed in?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In intelligence offensive work or intelligence counter -- or offensive counter-intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly make a distinction between offensive intelligence work and offensive counter-intelligence work?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Offensive counter-intelligence [as interpreted] work involves gathering intelligence in foreign countries or about foreign countries or about foreign subjects abroad. The purpose is to discover their secrets and to inform the political leadership of their secrets. So this is a manner of discovering enemy secrets. But offensive counter-intelligence work is part of that activity and only relates to the forces and means that a foreign country uses to obtain intelligence of ones -- regard -- relating to one's home country. So one tries to discover who the associates are of foreign intelligence services. One tries to discover to what extent and how they managed to infiltrate our intelligence service. Offensive counter-intelligence work always yielded the best results. So it's -- the best thing is to have an associate in a foreign intelligence service who will obtain information, so this has been proven to be the case on numerous occasions. And this is a system that has always applied whenever possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, Mr. Petrovic, reading the answer, you asked the witness to make a distinction between "offensive intelligence work" and "offensive counter-intelligence work." The answer reads offensive counter-intelligence work involves ..." and then it's described what is involved. And then it continues: "... but offensive counter-intelligence work is part of that activity," which is not very clear and is not distinguishing between what you asked the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Your Honour, at the beginning of the answer, it should say "offensive intelligence" not "offensive counter-intelligence." That is at page 59, line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The interpretation has been corrected and my question is therefore moot. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's please have a look at paragraph 363 now, in your report. Could you first tell us whether something is missing in the text. Here it says during that period his superiors were the assistant chief of the sector, the chief of the sector, the chief of the USDB for Belgrade, the chief of the RSUP of Serbia, and the republican secretary of the interior. Is there anything that is missing here in this list of those who were superior to Simatovic from 1986 to 1990?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistants and deputies are missing. The assistant chief, the deputy chief of the USDB for Belgrade. Here it says the chief of the RSUP of SR Serbia; it should say the chief of the RSDB of the SR Serbia. That concerns the chief of the service. So his assistant and deputy are missing, and then there's the chief of service, and then the minister. So there were seven other positions. I am not sure whether I have counted them correctly. I can count them again for the sake of the transcript, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Be so kind as to do that. In the first period, from 1986 to 1990, which positions were above the position that Franko Simatovic held?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, there was the assistant chief of the USDB for Belgrade, there was the deputy chief of the USDB for Belgrade, there was the assistant chief of the RDB of the SUP, and there was the deputy chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the chief of the RSUP -- I'll repeat this again. First of all, he had the assistant to the chief of the sector. And then there was the chief of the sector. That's the second position. Then there was the assistant who covered that field in the USDB, the assistant chief. And then there was the deputy chief of the USDB. And then the chief of the USDB. Then the assistant of the chief of the RDB. We had the RDB. Then the deputy chief of the RDB. And then it says the chief of the RSUP of SR Serbia. It should say "the chief of the RDB of SR Serbia." And then there was the minister, the republican secretary for internal affairs. That was the title at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we should now look at paragraph 364 relating to the duties and responsibilities of the head of section, which is the position occupied by Simatovic from 1990 to 1992. Since there are inconsistencies in the text itself, could you please, starting from "head of group" until "republic secretary," enumerate, slowly, the levels above "head of group" for the record.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relative to the head of group, there was assistant chief of sector, because the group is part of the sector, although already in this paragraph they talk about "section," but it's the same thing. So head of group. Then assistant chief of sector. Then chief of sector. Then assistant chief of the administration of the SDB for Belgrade. Then deputy -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning, please. Explain slowly. The interpreters can really not follow the speed at which you speak.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the first level above the chief of section, his first immediate superior, is assistant chief of sector. The next level is chief of sector. The next level is assistant chief of the department of state security for Belgrade. The next level is deputy chief of the administration of state security for Belgrade. The next level is chief of the administration of state security for Belgrade. The next level is assistant chief of the State Security Service, at the republic level. The next level is deputy chief of the State Security Service, and above him is the chief of the State Security Service. And the last, the highest one, is the republic secretary for internal affairs, which means the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Could we now look at paragraph 365. It refers to the position of deputy chief of the administration. It says he did not run the service independently, except in the absence of the chief. You have reviewed the personnel file of Mr. Simatovic. While he was deputy chief, was there all the time a chief of administration -- of the 2nd Administration of the RDB all the time?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was the chief of administration. In fact, there were two chiefs of that administration within that period. Do I need to name them?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We can see that in paragraph 370 of your report. I should now like to ask you to tell us about the deputy chief. How many levels were above him, that is to say, between him and the minister, at the time when Simatovic was deputy chief of the 2nd Administration?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question again, for the record, so I answer carefully?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So, at the time when Simatovic was deputy chief of his administration, how many levels of management were between him and the minister of the interior? Just list the positions, and we'll count them ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, we are now talking about levels, levels, levels. Is there any dispute about the organigram of who was in a higher hierarchical position, which doesn't answer any question on -- on who did what, but about hierarchy organigram structure?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No dispute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you have kept us busy now for five to ten minutes on a matter which is not in dispute. And apart from that is -- I mean, five levels, what is still missing is to see where someone is in the organisation apart from looking what is still above him. You should also look at what is beneath him so that you ... but there is no dispute about that. What are we doing? I mean, you have a report. It says what the position of Mr. Simatovic was. There's no dispute about the hierarchical structure, how many positions were above him. So why do we have to listen to all that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I agree with you completely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... then please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- we all remember the instructions -- just one sentence, please. We all remember the instructions from the Trial Chamber to indicate which parts of the report were not in dispute. Unfortunately, we never agreed about this. That is why this remained unclear, but I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this is not part of the report. What you are eliciting is evidence which goes beyond what is found in the report, and apparently there is no dispute about that. I do not know how intensive the negotiations have been on all these levels, whether you ever discussed it. I'm looking at you -- I'm looking at you, Ms. Marcus. Was the number of levels ever discussed to seek an agreement on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We didn't discuss it specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. And there's no dispute. It's not even worth discussing. And we are kept busy with it for I don't know exactly how many minutes, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am going to conclude very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 366, you write Franko Simatovic, speaking of his position of deputy chief of 2nd Administration, you say he had a pretty lowly position or a relatively low position. Why do you designate it as relatively low?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there were several more positions above that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 369. In fact, before that, let me ask you this: Was it possible that somebody holds two jobs in the service at the same time; for instance, special advisor and deputy chief of administration?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, its completely impossible for anyone to cover two jobs at the same time because they would have two letters of appointment, two salaries. They would have to pay double contributions for pension and other benefits, et cetera. That is absolutely impossible under the Law on State Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in the documents you reviewed out of the personnel file of Mr. Simatovic, did you ever find an appointment of Mr. Simatovic as chief of the personnel administration of RDB?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's move to paragraph 372. In that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my question on page 65, line 8, refers to personnel administration and Simatovic as its chief, whereas I was asking about the personnel file of Mr. Simatovic, and the position involved was chief of the 2nd Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We are coming back to paragraph 372. Here, in the context of the establishment of the unit for anti-terrorist actions, you refer to the decision of the minister of the interior to establish special units of the police. Why is this decision of the minister to set up special units of the police important in the context of the JATD?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It preceded the establishment of the unit for anti-terrorist action. The situation was that by his legal authority the minister of the interior formed special units of the police. As we see here, the strength was 15 detachments, and he filled them - among others - with members of the police and the reserve force of the ministry. That was happening in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When drawing up your report, did you have at your disposal any documents relating to the establishment of the unit for anti-terrorist action JATD, or did you make your conclusions about the establishment of this unit in some other ways?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to draw my conclusions in a round-about way, because I did not see the decision to establish the JATD specifically. Rather, based on personnel files and other decisions, including letters of appointments and assignment and the payrolls, I reconstructed the moment when they were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at P3039. This document provides a few examples, or, rather, samples, bearing purportedly Simatovic's signature taken from several lists of per diem payments, and it is not in dispute that it says "deputy commander of JATD," and Simatovic puts his initials and writes: "On behalf of the commander of the JATD." On behalf of the commander. The parties agree that it is not in controversy; that it says "deputy commander," in fact. For what reason and in what circumstances does one put this addition "za" before a signature?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a person other than the one indicated in the typewritten signature is signing. If that person whose name is typewritten is not in a position to sign himself, then somebody else is signing for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If Simatovic had been deputy commander of the JATD, would it have been necessary to put "za," meaning "for"?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. When somebody is higher in rank in hierarchy, he would sign himself, and he certainly wouldn't need the word "for." This happens only when somebody of lower rank is signing, even in normal office work. Of course, I have to state the reservation that I'm not an expert in signatures. I'm just trying to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm certainly not asking you about facts, Mr. Milosevic, just about the practice and the procedure regarding the signing of documents in the service and in state administration generally. My question was, since it's not very clear in the record: If Simatovic had been the commander of JATD, would he be signing with this word "za" any document?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is my last question. Look at paragraph 378 dealing with the JSO as a separate organisational unit within the department. According to what you have seen, was JATD also a separate organisational unit within the RDB?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I waiting for something or should I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat. What is the status of the JATD in the state security department?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a special organisational unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for Mr. Milosevic. But I would request that the report drafted by Mr. Milosevic be admitted into evidence as well as the annexes to that report, and I would also request that the documents on the basis of which this report was drafted also be admitted. And they have been referred to in the footnotes of the report. This obviously concerns only the documents that haven't already been admitted in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a list of those? Or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honour, no, we don't have such a list, but we will compile such a list. I apologise for that. And this is the best approach that you have suggested, and we omitted to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise the Chamber or the Registrar would have to go through all the footnotes, find out where the doubles are, find out what is already admitted into evidence. That seems not to be the right approach. We are waiting for your list. As far as the admission of the report is concerned, any ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps the report could be MFI'd. I'd like to have the opportunity to express our position at the tail-end of the witness's testimony. So if it could be MFI'd for now, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We take no position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the report itself, Madam Registrar, do you have the -- yes, you have the number. It would receive what exhibit number or what number to be MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Report number 2D913.1 will receive number D795, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Before we continue, could I ask one question seeking clarification of an answer of the witness. In relation to P1079, do you remember that you have seen a document in which it was described that Arkan had killed a volunteer and that it said that the SUP organs established that the volunteer, which was mentioned by name, that the volunteer was being provided with medical treatment? Do you remember that question? Do you remember the document? Otherwise we'll ask it to be on the screen. It's P1079, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I read part of your answer as it has been put on the record now. You said: "As I said yesterday," and you were referring to the raw information, "he can't change or alter anything in any way. But after that stage in the second part, he stands back a bit ..." And you have the document, and I think we need this second page. At least in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the document is under seal. I should have remembered that. You said: "... after that ... he stands back a bit because the information has been partially checked. He partially checked some of the information that he obtained. And he determined that with respect to one piece of the information provided -- well, that information was quite simply true." If you were referring to that person by the name of Kedo being killed by Arkan, then I'm surprised if you would have said that information was quite simply true, because from what follows one would be more inclined to conclude that it was untrue that he was killed. Could you clarify this? Or is it a mistake in translation or transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a mistake in interpretation and in the transcript. It should say it was determined to be untrue, "false," not "true." So checks were carried out, verifications were made, and it proved to be untrue. This was done in security organs. The technology is the same. So it was proved to be false. Something was partially checked and proved to be incorrect, and others things were being checked. So this report consists of two parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you -- first of all, do you know whether Mr. Kedo was killed by Arkan or not or whether he survived these days when they were sent to -- I think it was to Erdut? Do you have any knowledge about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I know nothing about that. I'm just commenting on what I have read here. I have never heard that name before. I was speaking about the procedure, the technology involved in drafting a report. Not about that particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So whether the verification of the death was untrue or whether the report of the death was untrue, you couldn't tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I know absolutely nothing about this case. I was just mentioning this case as an example to show how one indicates that some information has been checked and other information hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So either the information is wrong or it has not been checked adequately and the verification is wrong. Either of the two, because it's contradicting information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already said, this report wasn't drafted as it should have been. The first part of the information is separated by the second part by a break, by nothing else. So the agent should have indicated that there was a note he wanted to make. The last part of the information of the report, the last two paragraphs, would then have been completely clear, and there would have been a clear distinction between the part where the initial raw information was provided and the part where the agent expressed his opinion formed on the basis of the information he obtained from his source. So there is only a break here that makes a distinction between these parts. Nowhere does it say that the agent is noting that there is an important distinction to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm asking you this question because the matter had been raised with Mr. Theunens at the time, Mr. Bakrac, and there we made a clear distinction between what the report says and what the witness can tell us. It is clear that there is contradicting information in this report. But the conclusion that the information is false - and would you agree with me? - depends on the accuracy of the verification. If the statement of the organs of the Ruma SUP are correct, the information was false. If this statement of the Ruma SUP was not accurate, the original information may be true and may not be true. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know if I have understood you correctly. In any event, this information, given the way the information was obtained -- well, the information was obtained in the way that it was -- it was conveyed in the way it was obtained. An agent carried out additional verifications through certain individuals and established that it was false, so perhaps those individual lied. I know nothing about the case. I was just talking about the processes, the technological process involved. I'm not a factual witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that you agree with my analysis that if the verification is not true, if that's a lie, then the initial information is not necessarily true but could be true or could be untrue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Ms. Marcus, we have only a couple of minutes left. If you have a few questions to start with, then we could use those seven minutes. If you think that you cannot start with a small subject, then we would leave it until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be happy to wait until tomorrow but I could -- I could -- I do have a few questions. It's entirely in Your Honours's hands. I would also ask, perhaps, if the witness would prefer, I could take the binders. If he's finished with the binders that we gave to him, I could take them. I'll hold them here and if he needs to look at them during the testimony, that's fine. It's both for his convenience as well as for security reasons generally, because many of them are confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you been able to go through the binders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I brought them with me, but I didn't know how to return them. I have them here by my side. I went through them. The official could take charge of them, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would give it to the usher that would then return it to Ms. Marcus. And if you at any moment need to consult her tomorrow during your further cross-examination, Ms. Marcus will provide it to you. Mr. Usher, could you please assist. Ms. Marcus, if you have a few questions, please start.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you don't understand or can't hear me clearly at any point, please just let me know.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that you never attended a collegium, that it was impossible for you to receive operative reports, that you did not have any professional contact of any kind with Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Simatovic, that you did not know anything about the professional tasks or duties of Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Simatovic in 1991 or 1992, and that you did not have a lot of contact with Prodanic, the head of the 8th Administration. So you are not an expert on the actual activities of the DB in 1991 or 1992; would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I should understand your question. I'm not a factual witness. I can't testify about what happened at the time, about what they did or about what anyone did. I've testified here on the basis of an expert report that I compiled. I think you fully understand the distinction to be made, so I would not agree with your statement. That would also be the case if I had never worked in the service, but naturally it's better if someone worked in the service. But my expert report is not based on any personal experience. Otherwise I wouldn't be an expert witness, I would be a factual witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Marcus, is that what you meant to say, that when you said "you are not an expert on the actual activities of the DB," that you wanted to ask the witness whether he could testify as a witness of fact on the activities developed in the DB in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think matters are clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And just to make sure that we understand this clearly: Since my question only pertained to 1991 and 1992 - because that was what you testified to yesterday - I wanted to ask you about the latter period. Would the same -- would your same position apply to the latter period relevant to the indictment, that would be 1993 to 1995. During that period as well, isn't it the case, then, that you do not have any factual information on the actual activities of Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Simatovic during that latter time-period?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There's no difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, the title of your report is "Study on the Discharge" - that, I think, is "vrsenje" in B/C/S - "of Internal Affairs and on the State Security System." This title strongly suggests that you will be studying and analysing how the DB actually discharged its duties, not only what the duties were pursuant to the rules and regulations which would have been applicable. Since you've testified that your task was actually purely to rely on the laws, rules, and regulations rather than on how those duties and rules were actually carried out in fact, it wasn't quite accurate to say that your study was on the discharge of internal affairs, was it?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. In the Serbian language we don't have a more adequate term to describe what is contained in the analysis. In fact, our language is poor. There is not a good term for this. But I think that we understand each other. The duties of the service are carried out on the basis of the rules mentioned. It can't be done otherwise, for acting in another manner would be a violation of the rules. So it's not possible to find a more adequate term in the Serbian language to refer to what I have been testifying about. But if there is another term, I would accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, we'll have to adjourn for the day. I should not forget, Mr. Milosevic, to instruct you that you should not speak to anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow in the afternoon. We adjourn until Thursday, the 3rd of May, quarter past 2.00 - Courtroom II - in the afternoon.
